description: Open the window across Friday and Saturday. Renovate's own guidance is to `Avoid schedules like "Run Renovate for an hour each Sunday" as you will run into problems`, and the mechanism behind that is easy to miss: a schedule never starts a run, it only tells a run already under way whether it may act. Mend's cloud schedules jobs every four hours, so a window narrower than that interval can fall entirely between two of them. Sunday 21:00 to midnight in Tokyo is 12:00 to 15:00 UTC, and latex-release-action's jobs land at :41 past the hour, which puts 11:41 and 15:41 on either side of it. Four consecutive job logs from it and from latex-environment end in `Package not scheduled`, neither having failed at anything else, and both repositories spent three weeks with updates listed as awaiting schedule and not one pull request created.

Two days costs nothing to widen to, because the caps below are unlimited: the first job that lands inside the window drains the queue, and the eleven that follow it find nothing left to create. Width buys only the certainty that one job lands inside at all. Friday and Saturday here, Sunday and Monday in the elixir preset, so that the two families' pull requests -- and the CI runs they start -- do not arrive in the same burst against an organisation whose Mend plan grants one or two concurrent jobs.

The hourly cap decides how much of the queue escapes the window. Mend runs a repository's job every four hours, so the inherited limit of two pull requests per hour is really two per run, and a window holds about a dozen runs: a backlog larger than that never drains inside one, and what is left waits on the dependency dashboard until the next. Renovate sorts majors last, so they are what stays behind, week after week. Let the schedule alone bound the noise.

The concurrent-PR cap throttles the same queue from the other end. Majors are never auto-merged, so they stay open until they are reviewed; under the inherited cap of ten they hold the quota and the auto-merged minor/patch lane stops being refilled -- the same starvation as above, at a different valve. The window is the only throttle either limit needs to leave in place.

Refresh lock files weekly, in a narrow window on the first day of the one above. Bumping direct dependencies never rewrites the rest of the tree, so advisories in transitive packages accumulate unseen -- the eleven advisories found in ai-academic-paper-reviewer were almost all transitive. Lock file maintenance carries its own schedule that the top-level one does not override, so a window has to be named here; leaving it out would fall back to Renovate's Monday-early default and split the week into two update waves. Take the shape of that default -- one day, before dawn -- and move only the day. This lives in the latex preset rather than the npm one because the window is defined here, and it is a no-op for repositories that have no lock file.

Keep that window narrower than the two-day one above, because the reasoning for widening does not carry here. A version update is an item that a job can exhaust; lock file maintenance is the difference between the committed lock file and the registry. Merging it restores that difference within hours, so the next job inside the window has something to create again. Across 2026-08-27 to 08-29 that produced seven pull requests across the two repositories that carry lock files, one of them opened thirty-six seconds after its predecessor merged, each carrying a single transitive package where one weekly pull request would have carried all of them. Place it in daylight rather than making it wide. The interval between jobs is three to four hours through the day -- 07:57, 11:57, 14:57, 17:57 and 21:57 in Tokyo on 2026-09-04 for texlive-ja-textlint -- but it stretches overnight, and the first window tried here ran from midnight, where no job landed in it at all: the update sat under Awaiting Schedule for the whole of that Friday and the first job of the day arrived at 07:57. Reading a four-hour average off the Mend documentation was not enough; the overnight gap is what decides whether a narrow window is reachable. Six hours from 6am takes in two jobs, which is what one refresh needs -- the first creates the pull request, the second merges it once the checks are green -- and the third job, the one that would start the cycle over, falls outside. Nothing urgent rides on the cadence either: osvVulnerabilityAlerts in the default preset bypasses every schedule, which leaves lock file maintenance a routine refresh rather than the security net.

packageRules.description: Auto-merge minor base image updates, which nothing else here does. default.json covers patch and digest for every manager, and the github-actions and npm presets add minor for their own, so a Dockerfile minor was the one kind of routine update with no rule naming it: debian 13.6-slim to 13.7-slim sat open with `Automerge: Disabled by config` while an actionlint patch in the same window merged itself. Merging is not publishing -- an image reaches anyone only when a tag is pushed by hand (principle 6) -- and the build jobs prove the image still builds before this lands. Majors stay out, as everywhere else.

Order the texlive-ja-textlint tags correctly wherever they are referenced. The tag scheme is YYYY[revision-letter] (2025g, 2026a), which the default docker versioning mis-reads -- it treated bare 2025 as newer than 2025g. This rule lived only in the .github repository's own configuration, so every repository consuming this preset was ordering those tags by the default rules; it did not show because 2026e is currently the newest tag. The candidate filter keeps the alpine/debian/amd64/test/latest variants out, and requires the revision letter. A bare year is a real tag -- 2025 exists alongside 2025a through 2025i -- but loose versioning sorts it above every lettered tag of the same year, so leaving it in the candidate set would offer 2025 as an update to anything pinned at 2025c. Measured with renovate's loose api: isGreaterThan('2025', '2025g') is true. Excluding it is safe because nothing pins it and no later year has published a bare tag. The .github repository keeps its own copy of this rule in renovate.json, because it references the image from latex-build-modified.yml and does not extend this preset; the two are separate configurations for separate consumers, so a change to the pattern or the versioning has to be made in both. Both managers that see this image are covered: the Dockerfile FROM in latex-release-action and the container image in its test workflow.

Keep the shared-workflow reference on the moving v1 tag. Pinning it to a digest here does not create a review opportunity: moving v1 delivers the change to student repositories first, and Renovate only bumps the digest afterwards, so the pin makes this repository the last to see a change rather than the first. On the moving tag every consumer receives it at the same moment and the CI of the repositories that have one goes red immediately if it is broken. Third-party actions keep their digest pins -- those have an updater here and no consumer downstream.
